core: Working definition of consciousness: a person's awareness of themselves and their environment (APA working definition)
Levels of awareness: alert wakefulness, drowsiness, sleep, and altered states, each named with a one-line description
Awareness as a spectrum/continuum rather than an on-off switch
Attention as the spotlight of consciousness, with a limited capacity
The honest limit of multitasking: rapid switching with costs, not true simultaneity
Sleep as a changed state of consciousness (one line; full coverage belongs to the sleep sibling topic)
The unconscious in its plain descriptive sense: mental activity outside awareness
The honest note: the hard problem of consciousness — explaining subjective experience remains open
The honest framing: consciousness is the experience of having a mind

claims.claim: Consciousness is an organism's awareness of something either internal or external to itself; the lesson states the working definition as a person's awareness of themselves and their environment.
People experience different states of consciousness and different levels of awareness on a regular basis, and consciousness can be described as a continuum ranging from full awareness to deep sleep.
Wakefulness is a condition of awareness of one's surroundings (the high end of the spectrum), and drowsiness is a state of low alertness in which sustained mental effort is difficult.
Sleep is a circadian state characterized by partial or total suspension of consciousness and reduced sensory awareness — a changed state of consciousness, distinct from rest during wakefulness.

An altered state of consciousness is psychological functioning significantly different from ordinary states of consciousness; daydreaming, intoxication, and unconsciousness due to anesthesia are examples.
Attention is a state in which cognitive resources are focused on certain aspects of the environment rather than on others, and human beings do not have an infinite capacity to attend to everything.
Multitasking is studied as divided attention, and research attention in this area carries real implications — for example, the costs of multitasking in situations such as distracted driving.
Mental activity can run outside awareness: people can carry out complex routines, such as driving a familiar route while daydreaming, without being aware of doing so.

In psychoanalytic theory the unconscious is a region of the psyche containing content not directly accessible to awareness; this lesson uses only the plain descriptive sense — mental activity outside awareness — without psychoanalytic depth.

David Chalmers (1995) named the hard problem of consciousness: explaining mental functions is tractable, but explaining why they are accompanied by subjective experience remains one of the hardest open questions in science.

positions: Popular belief: people can do two attention-demanding things at once at full quality
Research view: attention has limited capacity; what looks like multitasking is rapid switching between tasks, and divided attention carries costs (e.g., distracted driving)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the honest limit: no one truly does two attention-demanding tasks simultaneously; the spotlight switches, and each switch costs time and accuracy. Sourced to the APA attention entry (limited capacity) and the Noba attention module (multitasking as divided attention with implications).

positions: Psychoanalytic sense: a region of the psyche holding repressed wishes and conflicts (Freud's dynamic unconscious)
Descriptive sense: any mental activity not directly accessible to awareness
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the plain descriptive sense (mental activity outside awareness, e.g., driving a familiar route while daydreaming) and explicitly notes that the psychoanalytic theory is a different, loaded sense. No Freudian depth is taught.

positions: Overclaiming headlines: science has fully explained consciousness
Chalmers (1995): mental functions are explainable (easy problems), but subjective experience remains the hard problem
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson's honest note is factual: researchers can measure brain activity, attention, and sleep, yet how subjective experience arises remains an open problem. The deeper mind-body debate is flagged as belonging to the philosophy subject.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Psychology 2e, Section 4.1: What Is Consciousness?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org serves a JS app, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2025id_/.../4-1-what-is-consciousness). Supports: consciousness as awareness of internal and external stimuli (internal: pain, hunger, thirst, sleepiness, thoughts, emotions; external: sunlight, room warmth, a friend's voice); different states of consciousness and levels of awareness experienced regularly; consciousness as a continuum from full awareness to deep sleep; wakefulness with high levels of sensory awareness, thought, and behavior; sleep as a state of low physical activity and reduced sensory awareness distinct from rest during wakefulness; other states including daydreaming, intoxication, and unconsciousness due to anesthesia; routines such as driving while daydreaming performed without awareness. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
